# Process intelligence in distributed cognition

The cognitive sciences inherited from their philosophical antecedents a tendency to localize intelligence — to treat it as a property residing within a bounded agent, available for measurement in conditions stripped of the context in which it ordinarily appears (Hutchins, 1995). What is striking here is that the empirical record on which the strongest claims for general intelligence rest is almost entirely a record of performance on artefactually decontextualized tasks, even as the same literature acknowledges, somewhere in its discussion sections, that the trait so measured fails to predict adaptive behaviour in the very settings that motivated the original construct (Sternberg & Grigorenko, 2002).

A different starting point — one that treats intelligence as a property of an unfolding process rather than as a quantity inhering in a substrate — does not deny that there are stable individual differences in performance, but it relocates the explanandum. The question becomes not how much intelligence a system has, but rather how its activity is organized over time, across resources, and in response to a medium that talks back (Clark, 1997). On this reading, the canonical findings from situated and distributed-cognition traditions are not boundary cases of a substantive theory of mental capacity — they are the central cases, against which the laboratory finding has to justify its claim to ecological reach (Hutchins, 1995).

The temporal organization of inquiry deserves particular attention. Notably, the timescale on which a process is observed substantially determines what kind of intelligence one is in a position to attribute to it; the same agent can appear rigid on the scale of seconds and flexible on the scale of weeks, or the reverse, depending on what counts as a unit of behaviour for the analyst (Thelen & Smith, 1994). What is striking here is that this scale-relativity has been treated, in much of the differential-psychology literature, as a measurement nuisance rather than as a substantive constraint on the very category being measured.

Taken seriously, the process view does not so much refine extant accounts of intelligence as displace them — and the work of replacement, rather than refinement, is what the chapters that follow undertake.

## References

Clark, A. (1997). *Being there: Putting brain, body, and world together again*. MIT Press.

Hutchins, E. (1995). *Cognition in the wild*. MIT Press.

Sternberg, R. J., & Grigorenko, E. L. (2002). *The general factor of intelligence: How general is it?* Lawrence Erlbaum.

Thelen, E., & Smith, L. B. (1994). *A dynamic systems approach to the development of cognition and action*. MIT Press.
